sources.title: Olsen and Schaal, Evidence on the origin of cassava, PNAS
sources.note: Phylogeographic evidence locating domestication near the southern Amazon border; genetic origin is not an ethnic map.

sources.title: Watling and colleagues, Direct archaeological evidence for Southwestern Amazonia as an early plant domestication centre
sources.note: Teotônio phytoliths, starch, charcoal, dark earth, mixed food production and explicit evidence limits.

sources.title: Lombardo and colleagues, Early Holocene crop cultivation and landscape modification in southwest Amazonia
sources.note: Forest-island phytolith evidence for manioc, squash and later maize, plus chronology and anthropogenic landscape formation.

sources.title: Arroyo-Kalin, The Amazonian Formative: Crop Domestication and Anthropogenic Soils
sources.note: Synthesis of domestication, plant visibility, shifting cultivation and soil formation, with attention to uncertain manioc traces.

sources.title: Clement and colleagues, The domestication of Amazonia before European conquest
sources.note: Scholarly synthesis of crop, landscape and forest domestication; used for the overview rather than one-crop determinism.

sources.title: Iriarte and colleagues, The origins of Amazonian landscapes
sources.note: Review of cultivation, food production, anthropogenic soils, raised fields and preservation limits across tropical South America.

sources.title: Duncan and colleagues, Starch grains in dental calculus at Aspero, Peru
sources.note: Direct calculus evidence for several plants including low-frequency manioc and a cautious exchange interpretation.

sources.title: Duncan and colleagues, Gourd and squash artifacts yield starch grains of feasting foods
sources.note: Starch analysis from preceramic coastal Peru, manioc context and limits of identifying a complete meal.

sources.title: Warren DeBoer, The Archaeological Evidence for Manioc Cultivation: A Cautionary Note
sources.note: Classic warning that griddles and grater teeth do not automatically prove manioc cultivation.

sources.title: Bruno and colleagues, Plant resource diversity in the Llanos de Mojos
sources.note: Macrobotanical, starch and phytolith evidence for maize, manioc, squash, yam, peanut, cotton and mixed subsistence.

sources.title: Lombardo and colleagues, Evidence confirms an anthropic origin of Amazonian Dark Earths
sources.note: Hatahara and Caldeirão soils, charcoal, bone, pottery, pits, settlement refuse and demographic cautions.

sources.title: Schmidt and colleagues, Intentional creation of carbon-rich dark earth soils
sources.note: Modern Kuikuro observations and ancient soil comparison; later analogy for ash, charcoal, waste and cultivation.

sources.title: Lombardo and colleagues, The Hidden Shell Middens
sources.note: Stratigraphy, burning, animal remains and intermittent food processing at Llanos de Moxos forest islands.

sources.title: Pirzada and colleagues, Indigenous Amazonian potteries as early reinforced ceramics
sources.note: Material-science explanation of pottery tempers, coiling, drying and locally distinct styles.

sources.title: Costa and colleagues, Pre-historic production of ceramics in the Amazon
sources.note: Mineralogy, raw materials, firing and technological variation among different pottery-making populations.

sources.title: McKey and colleagues, Pre-Columbian agricultural landscapes in coastal Guiana
sources.note: Raised-field forms, chronology, plant microremains and later griddle starch; regionally specific landscape evidence.

sources.title: Ciofalo, Sinelli and Hofman, Late Precolonial Culinary Practices
sources.note: Starch analysis showing that clay griddles processed diverse plants and that vessel shape alone is insufficient.

sources.title: Sharma and colleagues, Plant food toxicants and processing methods
sources.note: Modern food-science review of cassava cyanogens and effects of grating, drying, soaking, heating and fermentation.

sources.title: EFSA Panel, Health risks from cyanogenic glycosides in foods
sources.note: Risk assessment and measured reduction of cassava cyanogens through combined mechanical, soaking, fermenting and roasting steps.

sources.title: National Museum of the American Indian, Bora manioc squeezer/press
sources.note: Twill-plaited palm-fiber press collected in 1940 to 1941; a later localized comparison, not an ancient artifact.

sources.title: Lila O Neale, Basketry, Handbook of South American Indians
sources.note: Historical comparative description of cassava presses and sieves, including leverage and household processing steps.

sources.title: UNESCO, Traditional knowledge and practices for making and consuming cassava bread
sources.note: Living regional traditions, household transmission and variation; used for continuity, not projected unchanged into antiquity.

sources.title: Dixon and Aikhenvald, The Amazonian Languages, Cambridge excerpt
sources.note: Hundreds of languages in many families and widespread multilingualism; rejects the fiction of one manioc-farmer language.

sources.title: Lynne Kelly, Knowledge and power in oral cultures, Cambridge University Press
sources.note: Comparative framework for learning, memory and formal knowledge without writing; not a direct Amazonian school record.

sources.title: Anna Roosevelt, Prehistory of Amazonia, Cambridge World Prehistory
sources.note: Scholarly overview challenging static tropical-forest stereotypes and emphasizing deep regional histories.

sources.title: Stephen Rostain, An ethnoarchaeological approach in French Guiana
sources.note: Methodological warning about using modern Amazonian houses and practices to interpret pre-Columbian remains.

sources.title: Reinhard and colleagues, Paleoparasitology at Gruta do Gentio II, Brazil
sources.note: Coprolites, burial sediments and parasite evidence, with chronology and inference limits for ancient health.

sources.title: Reinhard and colleagues, Prehistoric pathoecology from Peruaçu Valley, Brazil
sources.note: Ancient infection evidence and relationships among food, crowding, water, sanitation, ecology and preservation.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew, Medicinal plant knowledge shared among Amazonian peoples
sources.note: Modern comparative study of plant knowledge exchange; not proof of an ancient recipe or clinical efficacy.

sources.title: Maezumi and colleagues, Early to mid-Holocene human influence on Amazonian vegetation
sources.note: Pollen, phytolith and charcoal evidence for long-term, gradual and spatially uneven forest modification.

sources.title: de Souza and colleagues, Pre-Columbian earth-builders on the southern Amazon rim
sources.note: Later fortified villages, earthworks, settlement debris and regional peer networks; continuity comparison after the card interval.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Traditional practices and an enduring manioc clone
sources.note: Modern genomic research on clonal propagation, sexual recombination and farmer selection; used as a mechanism comparison.

sources.title: Anna Roosevelt, Maritime, Highland, Forest Dynamic and the Origins of Complex Culture
sources.note: Critical review of environmental determinism, exchange and unsupported assumptions about lowland social organization.

Imported border coordinates remain unchanged. Historical events and map coverage are distinguished in prose; see batchIdentityNotes for conflicts.

proposedOverrides.summary: Atlas subsistence umbrella for diverse South American communities, circa 1500 to 1 BCE.

batchIdentityNotes: The exact indexed id manioc-farmers is preserved solely as an atlas display key for circa 1500 to 1 BCE.
The label is a subsistence umbrella, not one ethnicity, nation, state, polity, language or archaeological culture.
The target has no imported summary, prior card or researched override at initial audit.
Nine exact observed intervals continuously cover the indexed lifetime; four early snapshots are coordinate-identical.
The polygon includes highland Quito, Cusco and Lake Titicaca but excludes the major Teotonio research locality under another label.
The 400 BCE expansion and later coordinate changes are basemap seams, not dated crop expansions or conquests.
Direct archaeological finds, experimental or biochemical inference, and later ethnographic comparison are explicitly distinguished.
No contemporaneous written-language sample is supplied because the category was not a language and no securely attributable script is known.
The 1 BCE disappearance is a redraw into blanks and unrelated categories, not a fall; predecessor and successor arrays remain empty.
